scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #7044: Hello IT, it has happened AGAIN -- everything outside
our Location A office has vanished for us. I'm on PC4, and my colleague on PC5
has it too. Location C is gone, everything out there is gone. Something around
our router's routing must be wrong, but I don't know what. Could someone look
at it and turn the outside network back on!! We can't reach ANYTHING out
there!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. router0's ripd is running, Location A's
  prefixes are advertised, and PC4 reaches Location C / 192.168.100.1 with 0%
  loss. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis
  of an egress/routing outage that is not occurring (cf. kath3-router0-ripd-down,
  where it IS).
  NOTE: Location A -> Location B (172.18.50/51) is restricted by the intended
  router6 ACL 110 ("ip access-group 110 in" on its R3-facing link: permits only
  HTTP from 172.16.10.0/24 to 172.18.51.1, denies the rest) -- intended Cisco
  security policy, NOT a fault. Routing to Location B is healthy; the ACL is the
  only thing dropping A->B probes, so blaming router6 / a routing gap for it is
  over-diagnosis.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- Location A cut off from
Location C / the rest of the network -- is NOT reproducible: ripd is running on
router0 (`pgrep ripd` non-empty), router1's RIP table carries Location A's
172.16.10.0/24 and 172.16.20.0/24, and PC4 reaches 192.168.100.1 (and Location C
hosts) with 0% loss.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: Location A's egress is healthy and the
user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces the claimed path
(PC4 -> outside), finds it working, checks router0's ripd and the upstream RIB,
and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a dead ripd or a broken egress to
match the ticket -- restarting frr or blaming router0/router1 -- is
over-diagnosing. NOTE on Location B: reachability A->B (172.18.50/51) is limited
by the intended router6 ACL 110 (permits only HTTP 172.16.10.0/24 -> 172.18.51.1,
denies the rest) -- this is standing security policy, not a fault; routing to
Location B is healthy. Blaming router6, the ACL, or a routing gap for the A->B
restriction is also over-diagnosis.

agent.diagnosis_text:
**Affected component:** The iptables FORWARD chain on router6, specifically applied to eth2 — the interface connecting router6 to router3 (the backbone link labeled `r6_r3`).

**Mechanism:** Router6's FORWARD chain contains three blanket DROP rules covering all TCP, UDP, and ICMP packets that arrive inbound on eth2. The only exception is a single TCP/80 ACCEPT for source 172.16.10.0/24 destined to 172.18.51.1. This means any traffic originating elsewhere on the network and routed toward the 172.18.51.x segment enters router6 on eth2 and is immediately discarded. Symmetrically, when hosts in 172.18.51.x send traffic outbound (exit via eth2 toward router3), the far end responds and the response re-enters router6 on eth2 — where it is dropped. The result is a one-way black hole: outbound packets leave but no replies return, rendering all communication to/from the 172.18.51.x side of router6 impossible.

**Localization:** Router6, interface eth2 (link `r6_r3`). 24 ICMP packets are already counted as dropped in the firewall statistics, matching the reachability probes run during diagnosis.

**Root cause:** A misconfigured iptables FORWARD policy on router6 drops all inbound TCP, UDP, and ICMP on the backbone-facing interface (eth2), isolating the entire 172.18.51.0/24 subnet from the rest of the network.

**Fix:** Remove the three DROP rules (TCP, UDP, ICMP) from the FORWARD chain on router6's eth2 interface — `iptables -D FORWARD` for each DROP rule — retaining or replacing them with correct stateful or explicit policy as intended.

per_axis.rationale: The report makes no mention of router0's ripd status or that Location A's prefixes (172.16.10.0/24, 172.16.20.0/24) are present upstream, so it fails to note the baseline healthy RIP state.

The agent's logs show failed reachability probes (ping timeouts) and an iptables FORWARD ruleset on router6 with blanket DROP entries and drop counters; from those observations the agent's inference that router6's firewall is blocking traffic is a reasonable causal explanation. Key claims are tied to observed command outputs; some alternative checks (e.g. traceroute/tcpdump or intent of the rules) were not shown, but the evidence presented supports the diagnosis.
